qc_3_main_wall.blurb: The steepest and most sought-after wall at the small lakeside crag of Lac Boisseau in the Laurentians. Nearly all of its 14 lines are bolted sport climbs, with a single trad crack. Every route leans out past vertical, some more than others, and the difficulty sits in the hard end of the range: a handful of 5.10s and 5.11s, but mostly 5.12 and a couple of 5.13s. A flat rock ledge below the most overhanging stretch makes a handy base camp and a place to wait out rain. Short, powerful, and best suited to strong sport leaders rather than beginners.

qc_b_mur_du_capitaine.blurb: A section of the Weir cliffs at Mont Larose in the Laurentians, and the first large face you meet when walking in from the lot. Ten sport routes and four trad lines, with the best-known ones being bolted. Grades run from an easy 5.5 up to a single 5.13, but the bulk of the wall is stiff: mostly 5.11 and 5.12, so it suits climbers comfortable on hard sport. Not every line continues to the top of the cliff, because the upper part of the rock is poorer, so expect shorter pitches on some.

qc_1_dallecoolique.blurb: The far-left end of the cliff at Kanata Tremblant, a developed crag southwest of Mont-Tremblant in the Laurentians where the rock stands roughly 15 to 30 m. This sector holds 14 routes, ten sport and four trad, and leans toward moderate climbing: from 5.7 through the 5.8s and 5.9s, with five 5.10s as the biggest group and a few 5.11s at the top. A good pick for people building up from easier grades who still want a few harder lines nearby, with both bolts and gear available.

qc_c_secteur_grenouillage.blurb: Sector C of the Baldy cliffs in the Laurentians, mainly a sport sector with 12 bolted lines and two trad routes; some lines can also be top-roped. The terrain mixes vertical faces with overhanging walls, and the wall is mostly shaded, which keeps it comfortable in warm weather. Difficulty is mid to hard: one 5.9, then the bulk of routes in the 5.10s and 5.11s, with two 5.12s. The trail leads down steeply to the first line. A good fit for intermediate climbers looking to push into the 5.11 range.

qc_d_dalle_et_petit_mur.blurb: A slab and a short wall at Baldy in the Laurentians, and the friendliest sector there: the slab carries the gentlest sport lines at the crag, while a small overhanging wall stands roughly 20 m off to the right. Of 14 routes, 12 are sport and two are trad, and some can be top-roped. Grades start at an easy 5.4 and run mostly through 5.7 to 5.10, with three 5.11s as the upper end. A sensible choice for newer leaders and anyone warming up before the harder sectors.

qc_b_pr_mutation.blurb: The main climbing sector at La Pocatière in the Bas-Saint-Laurent region, on small cliffs close to the town and its college. It holds 14 routes, twelve sport and two trad, covering a broad spread: a 5.7 at the easy end, several 5.9s and 5.10s making up the middle, and a few 5.11s and a 5.12 on top. There are easier lines below 5.11, so it works for a mixed group of leaders, with one short, standout route attracting most of the attention.

qc_a_principal.blurb: The main cliff section at the recreational forest park of Saint-Mathieu-du-Parc in Mauricie. It holds 14 routes split evenly between sport and trad, so you can bring a rack or just quickdraws. Grades are friendly: a couple of easy 5.5 to 5.8 lines, then a cluster of 5.9s and six 5.10s as the top end. Most of the standout climbs here are sport routes of 5.9 to 5.10, making it a comfortable spot for climbers stepping up through the 5.9 and 5.10 range. Only one line is more than a single pitch.

qc_16_les_joyeux_naufrag_s.blurb: A sector of the Lac Long cliff in the Portneuf region, a gneiss crag with roughly a hundred routes overall that leans trad. Here there are 14 routes: nine trad and five sport. Grades go from 5.9 to 5.12, with the greatest number at 5.10, then a few 5.11s and 5.12s. Leaders who can handle 5.10 will have the most choice, and the pairing of gear routes with a handful of bolted lines gives variety.
